chapter_seo_title: Dao-Gui-Yi-Xian Ch.303: White Wuchang's Rope Trap & Bai Sai's Deception
chapter_meta_description: Li Huowang battles a hallucinated White Wuchang only to find a real rope strangling him. After freeing the Bai family, clan head Bai Sai's evasions draw Hongzhong's warning. 1.1K words.
og_title: The Wuchang Was a Lie, the Rope Was Real – Dao-Gui-Yi-Xian Ch.303
og_description: Li Huowang tears off his own face to escape a suffocating mask-illusion, then rescues Bai Lingmiao's family from wooden cangues—but clan head Bai Sai might be hiding more than he admits.
twitter_title: Ch.303: Fighting a Wuchang illusion while a real rope tightens. Li Huowang's rescue of the Bai family has a cost: a liar at the helm.
twitter_description: Li Huowang survives a hallucinated monster battle, frees the Bai clan, and immediately gets a warning from Hongzhong: Bai Sai is lying. Nothing is safe.

lore_anchors.definition: A folk-underworld emissary from Chinese mythology, depicted with a long red tongue; tasked with escorting souls—or punishing the living. Its appearance here masks a deadlier trap.
A heavy wooden pillory used in imperial China to restrain prisoners; in the Dao-Twisted World, being fitted with one marks the wearer as sacrificial prey in a ritualized game.
A Chinese folk expression of humble refusal; in this novel's universe, lifespan is a literal, tradeable resource, making the phrase carry genuine weight.

cultural_notes_faq.a: The monster was real in the sense that the attack was real, but its form was an illusion. Li Huowang was actually being strangled by a rope the whole time, with a wooden mask suffocating him. The Wuchang was a psychological layer over a physical trap.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Li Huowang's arm return but his neck wound remains?
cultural_notes_faq.a: The phantom self-mutilation (cutting off his arm) happened inside the illusion, so his real body was never harmed. The neck wound, however, was caused by the very real rope and mask, so it persists into reality. This is the novel's core rule: the threat is real even if its appearance is fake.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Who is Bai Sai and why does Hongzhong warn Li Huowang against him?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Bai Sai is the Bai clan head, a bearded, authoritative man who rescues Li Huowang from the questioning crowd. His explanation for the family's capture is vague and evasive. Hongzhong, Li Huowang's internal (and possibly supernatural) observer, calls him a liar.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What happened to the stone Bai Sai mentioned?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Bai Sai says his son found a "stone" that started all the trouble. Its nature and location are never elaborated in this chapter, leaving it as a deliberate loose narrative thread.
